enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

evidence_quotes.quote: The case of Kathmandu in Nepal presents a unique case to study this paradox.
The interviews were conducted in Kathmandu from May to July 2016.
Our method follows Lindseth & Norberg’s (2004) phenomenological hermeneutical approach.
The government does not have the capacity to provide safe water
Water price is going up and water availability is going down

country.comment: The empirical case study is conducted in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Introduction; PDF pp. 6–8, Kathmandu section and Methods

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative phenomenological study; Table 2 reports only NVivo statement counts across five themes (totaling 228 coded statements from 36 interviews) with no inferential quantitative effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Phenomenological hermeneutical analysis of Kathmandu resident interviews (36 coded interviews yielding 228 thematic statements across 5 themes: worsening situation over time [95 statements], blaming the water utility KUKL [58], high economic cost of poor water [29], daily coping with shortages [29], and lack of government capacity [17]) identifies a 'paradox of resilience': chronic delays in the Melamchi Water Supply Project, utility mismanagement/perceived corruption, billing without reliable piped supply, and lack of confidence in government capacity lead residents to absorb high monetary and emotional coping costs in an unregulated informal water market rather than mobilizing collective public pressure, masking growing vulnerability.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 9–15, Results and discussion, Table 2, Table 3, Figure 1; PDF p. 16, Conclusions

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (design ceiling for CASP Qualitative Checklist is 2): primary empirical data consist of resident lived-experience interviews documenting subjective perceptions and descriptive thematic links between delayed public water provision, perceived utility/government incapacity and corruption, ongoing utility billing without supply, and household reliance on unregulated informal vendors, while formal institutional/regulatory mechanisms (such as PPP contractual delays, KUKL complaint logs, and absence of vendor contracts/regulation) are cited from secondary sources rather than directly observed through administrative records or institutional fieldwork.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 7–15, Kathmandu background, Methods, Results and discussion, Table 2, Table 3

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines chronic public project/provision delays (Melamchi Water Supply Project), utility water bill collection without service alongside financial coping burdens, low formal complaint rates and lack of citizen participation/protest in chronic water shortage governance, and politicization/party patronage/unstable government affecting utility (KUKL) performance, alongside secondary discussion of unregulated informal cash water vending.
mechanism_flags.value: BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, delay, fees, complaint, participation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Introduction; PDF p. 7, Kathmandu section; PDF pp. 10–14, Table 3 and Results and discussion

outcome_flags.comment: Examines public access to water, intermittent/uncertain piped supply schedules, hours/days of supply continuity, chronic water shortages/scarcity, unsafe/poor water quality requiring boiling/filtering, household affordability/economic coping costs of tanker and bottled water, and multi-decade delay in public water supply delivery.
outcome_flags.value: water_access, service_reliability, service_continuity, service_quantity, service_quality, affordability, delay
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 7, Kathmandu section; PDF pp. 9–13, Results and discussion, Table 2, Table 3

publication_year.comment: Published in Water Policy volume 21 (2019), pp. 101–119, © IWA Publishing 2019.
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, footer; PDF pp. 2–19, running footer

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative phenomenological study based on two rounds of resident interviews analyzed with Lindseth & Norberg's (2004) phenomenological hermeneutical method in NVivo.

sample_size.comment: Methods (pp. 8–9) report 55 total respondents across two interview rounds in May–July 2016 (an initial exploratory round of 15–30 minute interviews on 26 May 2016, followed by 36 60-minute interviews in July 2016 transcribed into 40 hours of tape and coded in NVivo, yielding 228 statements in Table 2). Note that p. 4 informally refers to '50 people interviewed' as an illustrative figure in the narrative introduction.
sample_size.value: 55 local residents interviewed across two rounds (36 local residents in second-round 60-minute interviews coded in NVivo; 228 coded statements)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 4, Introduction; PDF pp. 8–9, Methods and Table 2

study_design.comment: Authors operationalize a qualitative phenomenological ('lived experiences') approach using two rounds of interviews with Kathmandu residents and Lindseth & Norberg's (2004) phenomenological hermeneutical thematic coding in NVivo to construct a narrative structure ('fabula') and causal loop diagram of social resilience.
study_design.value: Qualitative phenomenological study (lived experiences / phenomenological hermeneutical analysis of resident interviews to construct a narrative fabula)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 4, Introduction; PDF pp. 8–9, Methods
